### Existing parts the change reaches (compared old against new)

**A visitor tries bad sign-ups, signs up twice, and logs in with wrong details before logging in properly**
1. Sign up with an empty username (refused).
2. Sign up with an oversized username (refused).
3. Sign up with a too-short password (refused).
4. Sign up properly.
5. Sign up again with the same name (refused as taken).
6. Log in with the wrong password (refused).
7. Log in as an unknown user (refused).
8. Log in properly.
Why: changed route (sign-up and login call the changed hashing function). Statuses read from handlers.go.

**A reader adds books, puts one on their shelf, lists and removes it, and is refused without a valid token**
1. Sign up and log in.
2. Add a book, then add the same book again.
3. Add a book with too many tags (refused).
4. Put the book on the shelf.
5. List the shelf.
6. List the shelf with no token (refused).
7. Put a book on the shelf with a bad token (refused).
8. Remove from the shelf with no token (refused).
9. Remove the book from the shelf.
10. List books by tag.
Why: changed routes (everything behind the token check runs the changed hashing function); list books shares code with the shelf. Statuses from handlers.go and auth.go. The book list gets longer as data accumulates over the iterations of a pass.

**A reader reviews a book with good and bad ratings and text, then a second user checks the reviews and their own shelf**
1. Sign up, log in and add a book.
2. Post a good review.
3. Post reviews with a rating below and above the allowed range (refused).
4. Post a review with oversized text (refused).
5. Post a review with no token (refused).
6. List the reviews.
7. Sign up and log in a second user, who opens their own shelf.
Why: changed route (review create sits behind the token check); second user added for owner-scoped data. Statuses from handlers.go and auth.go.

### New feature (new build only)
None: this change adds no routes.

### Controls

**A visitor checks the service is up and opens a book**
1. Check health.
2. Sign up, log in and add a book.
3. Open the book.
Why: control (health and book detail are outside the change).

Gaps: none reported by validation. Sign-up, login and token checks are covered by happy, negative and edge-input steps.

**Method.** Baseline run twice (B1, B2) and candidate once (C), in the order B1, C, B2, sequentially on one machine. Three runs give no confidence interval; treat verdicts near the thresholds as uncertain.

Gated metrics decide the verdict. For each, the worse baseline is the larger of B1 and B2, the noise band is the difference between them, and the allowed rise is the larger of a fraction of the worse baseline and an absolute figure. A metric is a regression when the candidate is above the worse baseline by more than the allowed rise and by more than the noise band, and improved by the opposite rule against the better baseline. When neither holds and the noise band is larger than the allowed rise, no verdict is given (withheld): a change of the allowed size could not be seen in this run. Smallest detectable is the larger of the allowed rise and the noise band. A step that passed on both baseline runs and failed on the candidate is a regression. One gated app metric clearly better and another clearly worse is reported as a trade-off.

Allowed rise by metric: CPU per completed journey 20% of the worse baseline; Bytes written per journey the larger of 1% of the worse baseline and an absolute 1024; Write syscalls per journey 4% of the worse baseline; Open fds an absolute 1; Threads an absolute 2; Peak RSS 5% of the worse baseline; Heap objects allocated per journey the larger of 10% of the worse baseline and an absolute 100; Heap bytes allocated per journey the larger of 5% of the worse baseline and an absolute 16384; GC cycles per pass an absolute 2; Goroutines an absolute 1.

Latency is advisory: a latency or total CPU figure is called slower when the candidate is worse than the worse baseline run by more than 2 times the noise band (the difference between B1 and B2), by at least 20%, and by at least 10 ms (latency) or 0.5 s (CPU). It never opens an issue.

Gated metrics decide the verdict. **Method.** Baseline run twice (B1, B2) and candidate once (C), in the order B1, C, B2, sequentially on one machine. Three runs give no confidence interval; treat verdicts near the thresholds as uncertain.

Gated metrics decide the verdict. For each, the worse baseline is the larger of B1 and B2, the noise band is the difference between them, and the allowed rise is the larger of a fraction of the worse baseline and an absolute figure. A metric is a regression when the candidate is above the worse baseline by more than the allowed rise and by more than the noise band, and improved by the opposite rule against the better baseline. When neither holds and the noise band is larger than the allowed rise, no verdict is given (withheld): a change of the allowed size could not be seen in this run. Smallest detectable is the larger of the allowed rise and the noise band. A step that passed on both baseline runs and failed on the candidate is a regression. One gated app metric clearly better and another clearly worse is reported as a trade-off.

Allowed rise by metric: CPU per completed journey 20% of the worse baseline; Bytes written per journey the larger of 1% of the worse baseline and an absolute 1024; Write syscalls per journey the larger of 4% of the worse baseline and an absolute 1; Open fds an absolute 1; Threads an absolute 2; Peak RSS the larger of 5% of the worse baseline and an absolute 10; Heap objects allocated per journey the larger of 10% of the worse baseline and an absolute 100; Heap bytes allocated per journey the larger of 5% of the worse baseline and an absolute 16384; GC cycles per pass an absolute 2; Goroutines an absolute 1.

Latency is advisory: a latency or total CPU figure is called slower when the candidate is worse than the worse baseline run by more than 2 times the noise band (the difference between B1 and B2), by at least 20%, and by at least 10 ms (latency) or 0.5 s (CPU). It never opens an issue.
